data.title: Twenty-nail dystrophy (trachyonychia) — viva
data.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Twenty-nail dystrophy (trachyonychia)** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. What is trachyonychia?**
- Roughness of the nail plate due to matrix inflammation — opalescent, rough, sandpapered nails with excessive longitudinal ridging (opaque type) or shiny nails with multiple small regular pits (shiny type); when all 20 nails are involved — 'twenty-nail dystrophy'
- Commoner in children; usually benign and self-limiting

**Q2. Causes.**
- Idiopathic (isolated)
- Alopecia areata (most common association — especially children), lichen planus (most common histological cause), psoriasis, eczema/atopic dermatitis, ichthyosis vulgaris, IgA deficiency, vitiligo, sarcoidosis, pemphigus vulgaris, incontinentia pigmenti, selective IgA deficiency

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Spongiotic changes of matrix (most common — AA, eczema, idiopathic), lichenoid (LP), psoriasiform — nail matrix biopsy rarely justified because benign course and risk of scarring

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Onychomycosis (KOH), nail psoriasis (pits are coarse/irregular, oil-drop, onycholysis), LP with pterygium, brittle nails (onychoschizia), Darier's disease (red and white longitudinal bands with V-notching), chemical damage (nail cosmetics), ageing ridges

**Q5. Discuss nail pitting with causes (PYQ).**
- Pits = small depressions due to focal parakeratosis from the proximal matrix shed as the nail grows
- Psoriasis (coarse, deep, irregular, random), alopecia areata (fine, shallow, regular geometric grid), eczema/atopic (coarse, irregular, with transverse ridging), lichen planus, Reiter's/reactive arthritis, pityriasis rosea, secondary syphilis, sarcoidosis, normal individuals (a few pits)
- Rosenau's depressions (larger pits — psoriasis)

**Q6. Enumerate skin diseases with nail changes (PYQ).**
- Psoriasis (pits, oil-drop, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, splinters), LP (pterygium, thinning, ridging), AA (pits, trachyonychia), eczema (pits, Beau's lines, shiny nails from rubbing), Darier's (red–white bands, V-nicks), pemphigus (paronychia, onychomadesis), EB (dystrophy/anonychia), SJS/TEN (shedding), DM (cuticular changes), SLE (red lunulae, periungual erythema), SSc (pterygium inversum, ulcers), yellow nail syndrome, pachyonychia congenita, nail–patella syndrome (triangular lunulae, absent patella, iliac horns, nephropathy)

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — spontaneous improvement over years (children especially)
- Cosmetic: nail hydration (emollients, nail oils), avoid trauma, nail lacquer
- Active treatment rarely needed: potent topical steroid ± occlusion, intralesional triamcinolone to matrix, tazarotene; systemic therapy only if associated disease needs it (JAK inhibitors improve AA nails)

**Q8. Describe the two clinical types.**
- Opaque (rough, sandpaper-like) trachyonychia: severe, longitudinal ridging, opaque grey nails with brittleness and koilonychia
- Shiny trachyonychia: milder, many small regular pits that reflect light, nails shiny

**Q9. Is it always 20 nails?**
- No — not all nails need be involved; the term 'trachyonychia' is preferred; usually childhood; spontaneously improves in many (≈ 50% in 6 years), especially idiopathic and alopecia-areata-associated

**Q10. What is the best investigation?**
- Diagnosis clinical; nail matrix biopsy only when diagnosis influences treatment (lichen planus — risk of scarring/ pterygium); trichoscopy/scalp exam for alopecia areata; KOH to exclude onychomycosis

## Quick spotter facts
- Rough sandpapered ridged nails on all 20 nails of a child with AA — trachyonychia
- Fine geometric pits — AA; coarse irregular pits — psoriasis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Nail disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
